facts.raw_span: A 66-year-old man presented with a 24-hour history of incomplete closure of the right eye
flattening of the right nasolabial fold
right-sided hemiplegia rendering him unable to sit up or stand
The patient had a 3-year history of hypertension
no history of neurological disorders
The patient was alert and oriented
Effacement of the right frontal wrinkle
Incomplete closure of the right eyelid
Muscle strength in the right upper and lower extremities: grade 0/5
Hypoesthesia noted on the right side
Right Babinski sign: positive
Hemorrhage in the left thalamus-radiation crown region and in the lateral ventricle at 24 hours postonset

concepts.why: The patient presented with right-sided hemiplegia, incomplete closure of the right eye, and flattening of the right nasolabial fold, which are consistent with a left-sided intracerebral hemorrhage, as confirmed by the emergency CT scan showing hemorrhage in the left thalamus-radiation crown region and in the lateral ventricle.

The patient had a 3-year history of hypertension, which is a risk factor for hypertensive intracerebral hemorrhage, and the presentation of right-sided hemiplegia and incomplete closure of the right eye is consistent with this diagnosis.
The emergency CT scan showed hemorrhage in the left thalamus-radiation crown region, which is consistent with a thalamic hemorrhage.
The patient presented with right-sided hemiplegia and hypoesthesia, which are consistent with a lacunar stroke, although the presence of hemorrhage on the CT scan makes this diagnosis less likely.

The patient's age and history of hypertension are risk factors for cerebral amyloid angiopathy, although the presence of hemorrhage on the CT scan and the lack of other supportive findings make this diagnosis less likely.
The emergency CT scan showed hemorrhage in the lateral ventricle, which is consistent with a primary intraventricular hemorrhage.

The patient's presentation and the presence of hemorrhage on the CT scan could be consistent with an arteriovenous malformation, although the lack of other supportive findings makes this diagnosis less likely.

The patient's presentation and the presence of hemorrhage on the CT scan could be consistent with a cavernous malformation, although the lack of other supportive findings makes this diagnosis less likely.
